prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
Do NOT continue ciprofloxacin — confirmed precipitant of this crisis.
Do NOT delay intubation if respiratory parameters cross threshold; bedside intubation is safer than emergency intubation after collapse.

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical MG; reserve for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

key_clinical_evidence: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.

Myasthenic crisis = respiratory failure or imminent failure (FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP less negative than -30 cmH2O, weak cough, bulbar collapse) — ICU admission, urgent IVIG or PLEX, intubation criteria documented serially.
Ciprofloxacin is a well-documented precipitant of myasthenic crisis — FDA black-box warning since 2008.
Crisis management priorities: identify and remove precipitant, support ventilation, accelerate antibody removal (PLEX) or modulation (IVIG).
Cholinergic vs myasthenic crisis distinction: muscarinic symptoms (miosis, fasciculations, bradycardia, hypersecretion) suggest cholinergic; their absence and ongoing weakness suggest myasthenic.

patient.history_present_illness: A 55-year-old woman with known myasthenia gravis (in stable remission on pyridostigmine for 2 years) presented to the emergency department with acute respiratory distress and rapidly progressive generalized weakness. She had been doing well on pyridostigmine 60mg TID with minimal symptoms for 18 months. Four days ago, she visited an urgent care clinic for dysuria and was diagnosed with a urinary tract infection. The urgent care provider prescribed ciprofloxacin 500mg twice daily, which she started that evening. The following morning, she noticed her ptosis was slightly worse. By day 2 of ciprofloxacin, her ptosis was severe and she could barely see. By day 3, she was unable to lift her arms above shoulder height and had severe difficulty swallowing. On the morning of presentation (day 4), her husband found her unable to get out of bed, gasping for breath, with oxygen saturation of 86% at home on pulse oximeter. She denied any recent fever (only the UTI), no new medications other than ciprofloxacin, no alcohol, no change in pyridostigmine dosing. She had not informed the urgent care provider of her MG diagnosis. Her NIF is -18 cmH2O on presentation — at threshold for intubation.
